articles.title: Portland’s working waterfront is no place for professional soccer
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content: I love the Hearts of Pine. Been to my share of games. Have spent hundreds of bucks on gear. I’m on a first name basis with one of the owners. And I appreciated the statement they made last month calling for accountability after ICE murdered Johan Sebastian Guerrero Duran. All that said, the city of Portland should not carve out an exception to our working waterfront zone in order to allow them to build a $50 million dollar soccer stadium on land protected for marine-based industries. Why? Well, soccer stadiums can operate anywhere. Cargo ships, barges, trawlers, and tugboats cannot. Nor can the longshoremen and women, stevedores, harbor pilots, and deckhands who service them. They need deep water ports, which is what the western waterfront provides. As background, a couple weeks ago, the Hearts of Pine announced they had put Cassidy Point, the westernmost corner of our waterfront, under contract to build an 11,000 seat soccer stadium. That sale is contingent on the city approving a carveout to our longstanding protections for marine-based freight and industrial uses, which need access to the deep water of the harbor. The zone was first put in place in the late 1980’s after a developer transformed Central Wharf into a string of 150+ high-end condos (now called Chandler’s Wharf). The backlash to that development led to a citizen referendum in which Portlanders voted 2-1 to freeze all non-marine development on the water side of Commercial street. That zoning has been modified carefully over the years, and only after extensive input from those working the piers. Those modifications have allowed for a certain percentage of non-marine uses, mostly on the upper floors of old or new structures, in order to provide some economic diversity. Overall, the amount of space in Portland that marine business can use is decreasing . But for the western half of the waterfront, where the Hearts of Pine want to build their stadium, there’s been some real growth in marine industries. Eimskip, a shipping company, moved into the International Marine Terminal at the beginning of the western waterfront in 2013. Around the same time, Portland Yacht Services turned 23 acres of what was fallow land into a thriving boat restoration and storage business. And between those two sites, a massive cold storage facility was built. This has meant hundreds of new good-paying jobs, doing exactly the work that can only be done on the waterfront. A real success story of how protecting land for its best community use, not simply its most profitable return for an investor, can help everyone. But Cassidy Point was recently purchased by a multi-billion dollar out-of-state hedge fund . Those investors have reportedly been trying to make a quick buck by flipping it. Apparently, both the Maine Port Authority and Eimskip had been interested in buying it before the hedge fund, because they had wanted to expand commercial shipping to that area. But my guess is the hedge fund managers know that if they could find a buyer who would seek to rezone the property out of its protected status, they could exponentially maximize their profit (some estimates say eliminating its protected status inflates the value ten times). That’s where the Hearts of Pine came in. When I was mayor, Portland developed a comprehensive plan where groups from all across the city came together to discuss what we wanted to see for Portland by 2030. Fully 91% of Portland residents surveyed at the time supported “continued protections for Portland’s working waterfront.” That is why two of the plan’s major goals for the waterfront are the “ … mitigation of market trends that could compromise the balance between marine industries and competing development,” and “recognize and reinforce waterborne transport of goods and people as foundational to our community.” Even in our most recent overhaul of our building code, the waterfront protection zone, in its entirety, was kept intact. So, what to do? Clearly we love our soccer team. And if the owners want to spend their own money building a new stadium, they certainly have that right. But, as I said above, soccer stadiums can go anywhere. They could put it out on Riverside Street (hey, if it is good enough for our homeless shelter, it should be good enough for soccer). Or maybe next to 295, just up from Cassidy Point, where there are huge swaths of land near going unused. The Hearts of Pine owners said they actually looked at 12 viable sites. But wherever it goes, it should not go on the waterfront. Supporting the home team matters, but in this case, the home team I side with are the women and men who need the waterfront to make a living. *** This story was originally published by The Beacon , a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from the Beacon, sign up for the free Beacon newsletter here . The post Portland’s working waterfront is no place for professional soccer appeared first on Pine & Roses .

articles.title: Milwaukee Socialist Organizer Class – Register by October 4th!
articles.author: Milwaukee DSA
articles.content: Are you interested in becoming the best organizer you can be? Do you want to expand socialism here in Milwaukee, but are unsure of where and how to start? Have you been involved but feel like the project did not go anywhere? If you answered yes to any of these questions, the Milwaukee Socialist Organizer Class is for you! This eight week program will focus on holistically teaching you to be an unstoppable organizer who builds socialism, changes hearts and minds, and impacts our city. You will learn direct action organizing , as defined by Organizing for Social Change: Midwest Academy Manual for Activists, in which we organize actions, campaigns, and tactics to “1) win real, immediate, concrete improvement in people’s lives . . . 2) Give people a sense of their own power . . . 3) Alter the relations of power.” Interested individuals will register ( Click here , which is due by 11:59 p.m. on Sunday, October 4th, 2026), be contacted, and begin attending classes. DSA membership is not required to participate, but is encouraged. This education program will be a combination of in-person events with virtual events if necessary. Each unit will be roughly a week, with a week break in the middle of the program. Each unit will consist of classroom-style instruction in the unit topic (no more than 2 hours, which will be in-person on Monday nights from 7:00 p.m. until 9:00 p.m.), field work in organizing (which will be at least 3 hours and consist of having conversations, moving people to action, and building infrastructure for a strong socialist movement involving several types of campaigns), and time for personal reflection. Each participant must commit to the entire program and, unless excused, attend every unit instruction, and field work session. Missing more than three classes and field work sessions may result in removal from the program. This is the tenth time this program has been offered, and it is back by popular demand! The instructors have updated and revised the course to make you even more prepared to lead in socialism. Due to the nature of this program, we are only offering class in-person. Time commitment per week: Time commitment per week: Unit instruction: + 2 hours Organizing work: + 3 hours Miscellaneous tasks: + 1 hour Total time per week = 6 hour Weekly Schedule Class will be conducted on Monday evenings from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. and held at Central United Methodist Church (639 N 25th St, Milwaukee, WI 53233). Class will be in-person. Field work will be held at regular intervals over the week, with options to organize at several points during the week: (tentative schedule, subject to change . . .) Saturdays, 9:00 a.m. until 12:00 p.m. Sundays 12:00 p.m. until 3:00 p.m. Mondays 5:30 until 8:30 p.m. Program Timeline: Sunday, October 4th, 2026 at 11:59 p.m.: Application deadline – Apply Here! Monday, October 5th, 2026: Start of eight week program ( class held, 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.), held at Central United Methodist Church (639 N 25th St, Milwaukee, WI 53233) Monday, October 12th: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, October 19th: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, October 26th: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, November 2nd: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, November 9th: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, November 16th: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Monday, November 23rd: Class will be held from 7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m. Units Each unit helps to answer the question: what is organizing? Welcome: what is organizing? Get to know participants and instructor Define scope of class and intentions Determine goals and desired outcomes Organizing is one-on-one Conversations Learn the 7 point organizing conversation Practice the conversation and its elements Organizing is building the committee and the campaign The importance (or not) of the committee Power Mapping the campaign Strategy Chart Organizing is holistic productivity Traction versus distraction Time management and its importance The Reverse Calendar Overcoming blocks to action Organizing is a mindset Acknowledging hurdles and setbacks Failure is a great option Develop a practice to keep you going Organizing is raising money and managing it Why money is OK How to bring energy and money to your campaign The basics of campaign budgeting and finance Organizing is communications What does “messaging” mean? The power of media Writing workshop Organizing is bringing it all together You’ve got momentum – now what? Recap of unit themes Reviews Here is what previous students have to say about the Milwaukee Socialist Organizer Class: “[Before the class] I had no idea about the actual work of organizing. Now I feel confident that I would be able to become a leader in a campaign setting . . .” “I loved the practical application of socialism . . . [and] I loved the far-reaching application of some of the class content.” “This is a great way to move into the world of socialism. . . thank you so much for offering this course” “This [class] is a great first step for anyone looking to start organizing . . .” “I radically grew in my comfort around being upfront and simply being able to approach a complete stranger with a potentially controversial topic.” “New organizers and experienced organizers can benefit from this class.” “Generally speaking my confidence level just interacting with people about socialism has gone through the roof. I have been given a phenomenal overview of how to organize and I feel confident that I can find out what works best for me in the future.” “It was great to grow as an organizer within the confines of a welcoming community/instructor.” “I feel more confident organizing outside of an electoral context.” Meet your instructors: Alex Brower Alex Brower is a labor leader, socialist organizer, and Milwaukee’s 3rd district Alderman as a DSA endorsed elected official, serving on the City of Milwaukee Common Council. Professionally, Alex has been the Executive Director of the Wisconsin Alliance for Retired Americans, which organizes union retirees, in addition to other organizing roles with UFCW, SEIU, WisDems, and Wisconsin Jobs Now. In his organizing work, Alex has saved jobs from privatization, helped workers win a union voice on the job, defeated a temp agency, organized against a proposed iron-ore mine, helped bring comprehensive sex education to Beloit Public Schools, and won workplace healthcare for many uninsured MPS Substitute Teachers. As an MPS substitute teacher and former Milwaukee Rec. Department instructor, Alex brings a host of experience teaching others. Alex has also been a candidate for Milwaukee City Comptroller and School Board, running both times as a socialist. Andy Barbour Andy currently serves as a chapter co-chair of Milwaukee DSA. His DSA involvement began in the spring of 2023 as a regular volunteer for the Power to the People campaign, Milwaukee DSA’s now three-year-old campaign to replace We Energies with a publicly owned utility. After sharpening his organizing skills through regular canvassing and phone banking, he became a leader in the organization and has been closely involved in many DSA campaigns and projects. He’s been a consistent organizing force throughout his entire involvement in DSA. Andy currently also serves as chair of the Power to the People Working Group, though he’s previously held half a dozen other leadership roles in the chapter. Notably, he previously acted as deputy campaign manager of Alex Brower’s successful campaign for Common Council, where he oversaw the entire field operation. Any questions? Contact Alex Brower at milwaukeedsa@gmail.com Apply now! articles.title: Gloria Steinem Was No Enemy of the Left
articles.author: Daniel Geary
articles.content: In 2016, Gloria Steinem backed Hillary Clinton and dismissed young women who supported Bernie Sanders as doing so only because “the boys are with Bernie.” (She later said she misspoke). After her death last week, Steinem has been extravagantly praised in the mainstream media. Is it any wonder, then, that some leftists see Gloria Steinem as the “godmother of neoliberal feminism”?Yet left-wing dismissals and establishment celebrations both have Steinem wrong.At the height of her influence in the 1960s and ’70s, when she was a leading spokesperson for women’s liberation, Steinem was very much on the Left. Far from representing feminism for the 1 percent, Steinem believed that feminism had to represent all women and fundamentally remake society. Like many other major figures of second-wave feminism, she backed far-reaching reforms of the kind that many on the Left today support: federally funded childcare, a generous guaranteed annual income for all, strong labor unions, and opposition to racism and militarism.Steinem is best understood as a left-liberal who sought transformative reforms within existing institutions. Working within established institutions hardly made her a tool of the establishment. Like Michael Harrington, she sought the “left wing of the possible.” Indeed, she remained closely connected to the organization Harrington founded, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), up until the moment she betrayed it in 2016 by backing Hillary over Bernie. Had Steinem lived in Europe rather than the United States, she would have been easily identified as a socialist. After all, at the height of the Cold War, she wrote her senior thesis on George Orwell, whom she praised as a “socialist libertarian.”Steinem is misunderstood partly because most historical accounts of the 1960s and 1970s focus solely on the growth of radical social movements, the implosion of Cold War liberalism, and the conservative backlash, erasing the extent to which many American liberals became radicalized during this period. In 1972, the Democratic Party nominated the most left-wing candidate in its history. George McGovern captured the nomination by mobilizing the energies of the antiwar, civil rights, and feminist movements. He advocated defunding the military-industrial complex to meet pressing domestic needs such as childcare provision and fighting poverty and racial inequality. Steinem was closely allied to McGovern, though she outflanked him on the left.Both before and after her public embrace of feminism in 1969, Steinem was a central player on the leftmost wing of the Democratic Party. She was a vital broker — of ideas, organizations, and people — who connected social movements to mainstream political institutions and helped make a space where the Left and liberalism could meet.By the late 1960s, Steinem had become a prominent political activist. She helped organize a February 1968 advertisement of four hundred writers and editors who protested the Vietnam War by pledging to withhold 10 percent of their federal income taxes (the estimated amount of the federal budget devoted to the war). She worked tirelessly on behalf of the United Farm Workers (UFW), an insurgent labor union organizing migrant farm workers in California and employing national boycotts of non-union-harvested produce. Steinem wrote press releases for the union, raised money for its activities, and used her connections to help place UFW leader Cesar Chavez on the cover of Time.Steinem also worked with Local 1199, the hospital workers’ union key to progressive politics in New York City. The predominantly African American and Puerto Rican workers whom 1199 organized were, she wrote, like farmworkers, “systematically excluded from 35 years of protective labor legislation” and had been “blackmailed into subsidizing society with unpaid labor.” To Steinem, it was “more and more clear that there has to be a new wave of labor organizing as far-reaching as in the thirties, but this time including all those who have been unprotected by legislation and unions: migrant workers; hospital and domestic workers; all the invisible poor.”In 1969, Steinem announced that she was joining the feminist movement and quickly became its best-known spokeswoman. In this role, she advocated not just gender equality but the broader goals of equality and justice for which she had long fought. Steinem declared feminism “an integral part of rescuing this country from its old, expensive patterns of elitism, racism, and violence.” Feminists, she pronounced, were “not interested in imitating the inhuman male role, but in revolutionizing society.”Steinem took seriously the notion that feminism needed to represent all women. Keen to spread her message, she conducted a series of widely attended “Women’s Liberation Speaking Tours” across the country. She always spoke alongside a black woman in order to establish the diversity of the women’s liberation movement, publicize African American feminism, and underline that the feminist movement’s goals were inextricable from those of the black freedom struggle.Achieving feminism’s goals, Steinem claimed, required significant reform of capitalism. The recognition of women as “full human beings” required paying them equally for their work, including compensating housewives for their domestic labor. Steinem’s economic model was Sweden. Then under the leadership of Olof Palme, Sweden pursued both redistributionist policies and feminist ones such as free childcare and giving housewives the right to receive a percentage of their husbands’ income. Sweden, Steinem claimed, “is so far ahead of us . . . that Swedish statements on sex and equality sound like bulletins from the moon.”Steinem’s efforts to transform American politics in a feminist and left-liberal direction were embodied in the National Women’s Political Caucus (NWPC), the organization that she helped found in 1971 along with Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, and Betty Friedan. The NWPC’s founding statement of purpose had the far-reaching ambition of utilizing women’s political power for “the elimination of sexism, racism, violence and poverty” from American society by forming “coalitions with other oppressed groups.” It advocated housing for all, reform of the criminal justice system, comprehensive health care, a guaranteed annual income, the right for all workers to unionize under the National Labor Relations Act, and “an end to war.”Achieving such aims, they recognized, would be expensive. However, they asserted that the country’s “enormous resources” were sufficient if they were “reordered to pay for life instead of for death.”Steinem also advanced her left-liberal views in her most lasting achievement: Ms. magazine. Far from simply advocating individual change for middle-class women, the early issues of Ms. advanced a broad left-liberal agenda. The first issue contained articles on abortion rights, the housewife role, raising children without sex roles, and a piece by Pentagon Papers whistleblower Daniel Ellsberg on how macho ideas had driven the escalation of the Vietnam War. It also contained an influential article by Johnnie Tillmon, the African American director of the National Welfare Rights Organization who wrote from personal experience as a welfare recipient. Tillmon denounced welfare as a “super-sexist marriage” where you “trade in a man for the man.” She called instead for paying “a living wage for child-raising and housekeeping.”Steinem’s left-liberal views were typical of the women’s liberation movement. To be sure, a vocal group of radical feminists criticized liberals for working within established institutions. And some liberal feminists pursued women’s rights as an isolated issue. But the majority of feminists, including those in the NWPC, at Ms., and in the National Organization of Women, linked feminism to a broader program of social transformation that also targeted economic inequality and militarism.It may seem difficult to reconcile this view of Steinem as on the Left with the fact that in the late 1950s, she took a job with a CIA-funded organization that recruited young Americans to attend international Communist youth festivals abroad. Steinem’s involvement with the CIA was hardly admirable, but it’s not like she was planning the Bay of Pigs invasion. In any case, her association ended after she moved to New York City in 1962 to become a journalist. It is ridiculous to assert that Steinem remained a CIA agent who secretly worked within the women’s liberation movement to subvert it.It is fair to criticize Steinem for not being radical enough and for moving to the center in some key ways in her later years. But it is simply wrong to say that she “never shared” the goals of the women’s liberation movement or that she promoted a “conservative, anti-left feminism.” This mistaken view of Steinem reflects a misguided left-wing mentality that divides everyone into the “establishment” and “the radicals,” while ignoring the broad space in between. We should remember Steinem for having embodied a potent combination of feminism with left-liberal politics.

articles.title: Is There a Way Out of AI Doomerism?
articles.author: Garrison Lovely
articles.content: Not long ago, a close friend of mine, a software engineer, was discussing how his job role had changed in recent months as his company had moved to adopt an “AI-first approach.” He explained that this approach had altered his team’s dynamics. He told me how he now dreads one question more than any other, one that has become a refrain around the office: “Why don’t you just give it to Claude?” ‘It’ is usually a difficult engineering problem to solve, one that has stumped the team for a little while, or longer than a few minutes at least, often during a technical discussion that only a few years ago might have lasted well over an hour. Invariably, he will give the problem to Claude who, invariably, will produce an impressive solution within a few minutes. He doesn’t mind that Claude has provided him with a solution. He minds that those around him no longer understand him as an authority, as they once did. He minds that he now feels more or less fungible. Or perhaps, worse still, obsolete.The concept of human obsolescence is one that Garrison Lovely takes seriously in his study Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us — and How to Stop It. Rather than approaching the subject through the eyes of workers on the ground (like other recent books on this topic, perhaps most notably Sarah O’Connor’s We Are Not Machines), Lovely approaches it from above, with a bird’s-eye view, and as a problem of political economy. Obsolescence, redundancy, fungibility: these are political problems for Lovely. And yet those tuned into the noisy and ever-evolving discourse surrounding artificial intelligence know that most of the issues being discussed today do not run neatly along the usual political fault lines. Indeed, as Lovely acknowledges early on in his book, on what other subject do we find Elon Musk siding with the Service Employees International Union against Nancy Pelosi and far-right billionaire Marc Andreessen? Or Steve Bannon agreeing with Barack Obama’s national security advisor, Susan Rice, while openly criticizing Donald Trump’s policies?Lovely claims there is one matter everyone should be able to agree on, though: the fact that “a tiny group of people, backed by the most well-resourced organizations in the world, is attempting to render us obsolete.” Put like that, you might think the claim sounds tendentious at best (and, at worst, a sign of political paranoia). You might think that most of the artificial intelligence labs would recoil from such a description. But as Lovely is quick to point out, these companies have been remarkably candid about their ambition to do away with human labor.OpenAI, for instance, informs us in its charter that it has from day one been pursuing Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), which it defines as a “highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work.” No matter how the company phrases it, its mission to build AGI is precisely an attempt to turn capital into labor and remove one of the last remaining constraints on capital: the dependence on human workers. This leads Lovely to argue that AGI ought to be reframed “not as a new type of brain but rather a new type of machine, one that doesn’t make products or services, but produces labor itself.” He calls this machine “the Obsoleting Machine.”The first part of Obsolete, “What You’ve Heard,” succinctly catalogs the dominant positions on AI today. Lovely writes that “the roiling debate over AGI has roughly three competing camps: worriers, accelerationists, and critics.” The worriers, who include the AI-safety movement and those often pejoratively described as “doomers,” agree that AGI is possible but believe its development will likely have catastrophic effects on our future. The critics, who include figures such as Emily Bender (who famously cowrote a paper dismissing large language models as “stochastic parrots”), remain deeply skeptical that AGI is even possible (let alone imminent) and tend to dismiss the discourse around it as mere hype. Finally, Lovely speaks of the accelerationists (or “boosters”) who share the worriers’ belief in the technology’s remarkable potential but insist we should build out AGI as rapidly as possible. (Andreessen, for example, has gone on record to make the dubious claim that the longer we wait to build AGI, the more lives we lose that could have been prevented by breakthroughs in medicine.)The resulting alliances between these groups are often surprising. Critics and worriers, for instance, both want the industry restrained, although often on very different terms and for very different reasons; critics and accelerationists, meanwhile, can find themselves in agreement on the idea that hypothetical existential threats ought not to determine present-day policy and distract us from the here and now.Lovely devotes a considerable portion of his book to dismantling many of the concerns and arguments put forward by these camps (doing so very successfully in most cases) before proposing a fourth position with which he aligns himself, the “reformer.” AI reformers, he writes, “recognize that AI’s present harms and its potential catastrophes aren’t separate problems requiring separate approaches — they’re symptoms of the same underlying dynamics: competitive pressure, concentrated power, and a staggering lack of accountability.” Here he takes the well-reported examples of chatbots encouraging teenage suicides and the possibility of AGI posing a serious security risk if it were to slip from human control. Both emerge from organizations rushing to deploy systems they don’t fully comprehend.What might stop us from hurtling into the technological polycrisis Lovely fears? His prescriptions as outlined in the final section (“What to Do”) are commendable, but, geopolitically speaking, a lot would have to change before some of his demands could be met. Perhaps most ambitiously, he wants the United States and China to agree not to develop AI systems “designed to fully automate labour” until there is both public support behind them and broad scientific agreement about their safety. But for anyone who has heard the Trump administration’s repeated pledges to “do whatever it takes” to secure “America’s global AI dominance” and “win the AI race,” the likelihood of this happening might seem almost comically remote. (It’s worth adding that the Biden administration also treated AI as a race to be won against the Chinese.) There are other hopeful and more modest suggestions that might ameliorate the current situation. For example, the idea that we ought to build publicly owned compute infrastructure while establishing collective “data unions” to bargain over material to train the models. But if China was perceived as ramping up its AI operations, is there really a realistic world in which the United States wouldn’t follow suit and thereby abandon these fairer, more democratic ideas?There are times when Lovely’s book is frustrating to read. The overly unbuttoned style can grate or, worse still, undermine an argument (“neither side wants to create a rogue superintelligence or let any rando kill billions”). There’s occasionally a glibness to the prose (“Altman, like his chatbot, knows what to say to keep the conversation going — and your hands firmly away from the power cord”). And the structure of the book, with its many chapters, which are broken down further into sections and subsections, makes the experience feel like we’re barrelling through a textbook (one with some peculiarly cramped and sometimes unnecessary graphs and charts). And of course, there’s the rather sensationalist subtitle. But these are mostly minor (and editorial) criticisms.Obsolete does something both useful and challenging. It provides an illuminating snapshot of the current state of the debate on AI while proposing some sensible ideas on how to handle a technology that threatens to cause a lot of harm and entrench even greater inequality across the globe if left unchecked. But it’s unlikely to provide much cheer to those already feeling distant and alienated from their work, as they are asked one more time, “Why don’t you just give it to Claude?”

articles.title: How the Left Can Win a Supermajority
articles.author: Jared Abbott
articles.content: Adam Jentleson’s Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power challenges us to think longer term about what it would take to halt the steady march of right-wing authoritarianism and deliver durable but long-overdue relief for working Americans. Its premise is simple: the only way to get from here to a basically social democratic future (not his words) is to consistently win supermajorities in Congress, and the only way to do that is for Democrats to become competitive again in more red states. Flipping a six-to-three Supreme Court means holding the Senate across multiple cycles, which means maintaining something near sixty seats. In 2009, Democrats held at least one Senate seat in thirty-six states, including Nebraska, Montana, Arkansas, West Virginia, and both Dakotas. Today they hold seats in just twenty-four. Far too much Democratic strategy treats 270 electoral votes and fifty-one senators — or, on the Left, primarying centrist incumbents in solidly Democratic districts — as the objective. Picking off corporate Democrats in deep blue districts may be useful, but its strategic value pales beside beating more Republicans. Jentleson’s insistence that the real target must be 370 electoral votes and sixty senators should help to reframe debates across the coalition. His formula for getting there is simple: embrace heterodoxy. Jentleson’s prescriptions contain insights the Left would do well to absorb, along with blind spots that ultimately limit the book’s strategic power. The Working Class Is Not Left or Right Jentleson, a former top aide to Harry Reid and now president of the centrist Searchlight Institute, frames the challenge through a two-by-two grid, with economic issues (moderate or progressive) on one axis and cultural issues (moderate or progressive) on the other. “Right away, an important point jumps out,” he writes: “No box contains a majority of voters. In the United States, no single ideology can assemble a majority, let alone a supermajority.” And voters who register as “moderate” are not centrists so much as people whose views don’t fit neatly into left or right categories. Jentleson drives this point home vividly through his colorful descriptions of voters who embody a startling mix of left and right attitudes, like a twenty-four-year-old white Baptist in Nashville who cannot afford health insurance, hates the far-right influencer Nick Fuentes, wants Michelle Obama to be president because she embodies “humanitarian values,” thinks the United States should not be allied with Israel, has no problem with undocumented immigrants, and — wait for it — voted for Donald Trump. And, Jentleson correctly notes, ideological eclecticism speaks with a distinct working-class accent. Taking “a roughly equal mix of liberal and conservative positions,” he explains, is far more common among Americans without a college degree, and college graduates tend to be the only group giving ideologically consistent answers across the issue spectrum. Since working-class voters made up 59 percent of the 2024 electorate and since Democrats have been hemorrhaging working-class voters for decades, the fact that the Democratic Party is currently organized around the ideological habits of college graduates poses a grave structural problem that even the most successful efforts at turning out the base cannot solve. The Patchwork Party Jentleson offers an insightful, insider’s account of how Democrats switched from being viewed as the party of workers to the party of wokesters. Borrowing from the political scientist Ted Lowi, he argues that the Great Society’s shift from categorical, earned benefits — like Social Security and unemployment insurance — toward more discretionary, means-tested programs opened a vast field for advocacy, producing an interest-group ecosystem that absorbed functions the party used to perform itself. His history of the Democracy Alliance, founded after 2004 by rich Democratic donors from George Soros to Rob Reiner, traces how the organization was conceived narrowly as a vehicle for beating Republicans but evolved after 2010 into a “movement building” project for progressives, growing to more than 160 groups — some of which, like the Working Families Party, even ran candidates against Democrats. The Democrats, in short, had outsourced the party’s core functions to organizations with little stake in winning general elections and every expectation of a policy return on their investment, organizations that would not hesitate to cut off candidates who defied them. Candidate questionnaires became the shibboleth for winning endorsements and financial support from organizations in the progressive ecosystem that critics now collectively refer to as “the groups.” Jentleson’s illustrative case is the American Civil Liberties Union’s ten-page 2020 candidate questionnaire, a battery of yes-or-no checkboxes on a wide range of issues, backed by volunteers dispatched to press candidates at town halls. One of them even managed to extract a pledge from Bernie Sanders to let the Boston Marathon bomber vote. Jentleson shows the impact of this kind of advocacy by tracing the distance between the Sanders of 2016, who dismissed open borders as “a Koch brothers proposal,” and the Sanders of 2020, who raised his hand for decriminalizing border crossings, reversed himself on guns, and sat silently at a campaign event in Flint while surrogates spoke on his behalf, with his campaign explaining that “he didn’t want to speak on behalf of people of color when there were people of color on the panel.” He won nine nominating contests instead of twenty-three, as many working-class areas he had dominated in the 2016 primaries switched to Joe Biden in 2020. Which Heterodoxy? Which brings us to the central limitation of the book: Jentleson’s plea for heterodoxy is onto something important, but by not specifying which kinds of heterodoxy are up to the twin tasks of defeating Republicans in red states and delivering transformative economic policies for working-class Americans, he winds up championing a range of politicians who actively stand in the way of Jentleson’s own vision. Consider the roster of exemplars Jentleson gives. Mary Landrieu, whose Louisiana career opens the book, voted for George W. Bush’s tax cuts, voted to authorize the Iraq War, joined Republicans to permanently repeal the estate tax, and backed converting New Orleans’s public schools into a charter district over the objections of the teachers’ unions. Joe Manchin, the former West Virginia senator, shot a climate bill with a rifle in a television ad. John Bel Edwards won the Louisiana governorship by embracing fossil fuels and touting his business-friendly credentials. Several members of Jentleson’s heterodox Senate class of 2009 he himself describes as “business-friendly and fiscally conservative.” Now recall the two-by-two grid Jentleson used to open the book. The quadrant holding the most working-class voters who feel like they have no home in either major party is the one that leans left on economics and right (or at least not progressive) on culture. But most of the heterodoxy his book models — at least in the contemporary era — consists of Democratic politicians who are both culturally and economically conservative. That is the quadrant Democrats in red states have been targeting for forty years, but it has created a major strategic problem for the party. The heterodoxy of a Landrieu or a Manchin is certainly preferable to that of any Republican. But Manchin also torpedoed a rare shot at a broad economic program for workers not far from Jentleson’s own vision, and while Build Back Better had avoidable content and framing flaws that made it hard for working-class Americans to stomach, the man who killed it was Jentleson’s model heterodox Democrat. If the goal is more Democratic senators, that trade is worth making. If the goal is passing a New Deal–scale economic agenda to ensure economic security for all however, as Jentleson says his is, electing more Landrieus and Manchins amounts to a Pyrrhic victory, because they will undermine it at every step. The trouble is not that heterodox Democrats pick unpopular economics. It is that they tend to pick the least consequential items from a long menu of popular ones. Capping insulin costs, cracking down on price gouging, and trimming drug prices all poll well and surely provide relief to working Americans, but working-class Americans need more than just cheaper goods; they also need more leverage to bargain for better pay and benefits, and good jobs at a family-sustaining wage. And as we have found repeatedly in our research at the Center for Working-Class Politics , there is no tactical advantage to prioritizing more limited economic reforms over bold, visionary ones, so long as the latter are conceived in a way that taps into core working-class values of hard work and deservingness and, like Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s decision to pay for Social Security through a regressive payroll tax, effectively inoculates the policies against conservative attacks. Jentleson knows this, which is what makes the positive policy vision he offers at the end of the book somewhat frustrating. His American Security Guarantee promises social insurance sufficient to keep families from going hungry, access to public or private health care with expenses capped on a sliding scale according to income, and “a public service job if you cannot find work in the private sector.” He calls this platform heterodox, “embracing conservative values of personal responsibility, fiscal responsibility, and freedom of choice, while marshaling them toward the liberal end of ending poverty in the United States once and for all.” But those are not conservative values. They are working-class values, and they can be yoked to conservative, moderate, or progressive economics depending on how carefully it is done. This is exactly what FDR’s signature social programs and Bayard Rustin’s Freedom Budget did so well. So the heterodoxy Democrats need is not a grab bag of positions signaling independence. It is far more specific: Sherrod Brown– and Marcy Kaptur–style economic populists who pair culturally resonant positioning with a willingness to name their own party’s forty-year failure to deliver a better quality of life for American workers, and a program bold enough to rebuild communities hollowed out by decades of deindustrialization. Anything less would amount to a redux of Bill Clinton’s Third Way, which Jentleson rightly faults for offering limited redistributive policies like the earned income and child tax credits in place of a vision for improving the lives of working Americans, and which, like its 1990s predecessor, would end up feeding the far right it claims to fight. There Is No Substitute for Organization A key gap in the book follows from its own diagnosis of the Democrats’ shortcomings. Jentleson establishes, convincingly, that the Democratic Party has been hollowed out and its functions outsourced to advocacy groups, consultants, and donor networks. Didi Kuo’s The Great Retreat makes a similar argument at greater length. But Jentleson’s remedy is addressed almost entirely to individual candidates: say what you actually believe, and welcome the fight when the groups come after you. But what made Democrats viable in red states in the postwar era was not merely how they positioned themselves on the issues. It was the dense institutional web of civil society organizations that kept them embedded in and trusted by communities between elections. Lainey Newman and Theda Skocpol’s Rust Belt Union Blues documents how that social fabric operated in western Pennsylvania: Democratic-aligned labor unions sponsored the Little Leagues, ran the Labor Day parades, and published newsletters where people got political information they trusted. Being a “union man” was an identity, and it carried a quiet social expectation about which way to cast your ballot (i.e., Democratic). But as deindustrialization began ravaging rust-belt communities, unions funneled shrinking resources into emergency political advocacy, the Little League sponsorships ended, parades were canceled, local publications were suspended, and union halls were shuttered or turned into food banks. Newman and Skocpol’s crucial finding is that these communities did not become more culturally conservative. They were culturally conservative in the 1960s too. What changed was the political orientation of the key institutions of civil society. Right-leaning evangelical churches and gun clubs filled the vacuum, and they now perform the same function that unions once did, circulating political common sense through dense social networks, only in the opposite direction. With limited organic ties to local communities, heterodox Democrats in red states today can reach voters only through paid and social media. Given the extraordinary power of political polarization, they are unlikely to break through in a meaningful way without long-term, non-party-based community-building efforts. Rebuilding Democratic-aligned infrastructure in red states will take serious money and sustained commitment. Democratic campaigns spent billions in 2024 on advertising of uncertain value; a modest share redirected into a year-round presence in places the party has written off would be more valuable than any messaging memo could ever hope to be. None of this diminishes what Jentleson gets right. “Settling for smaller but ideologically purer majorities,” he writes, “is a path to purgatory at best, and losing to fascism at worst.” Fifty-one senators cannot rebuild the American social contract; sixty might. But a supermajority is a means, and Supermajority is far clearer about how to assemble one than about what it can achieve. The type of heterodoxy we need is a transformative economic program tailored carefully to tap into core working-class values and a serious investment in civil society organizations to help counter the hegemony of the far-right in red state communities. Without these two elements, Democrats may win sixty seats and once again have little to show for it.

articles.title: Britain’s Health Crisis Is Becoming a Political Crisis
articles.author: Jatinder Hayre
articles.content: Britain is becoming a sicker country. A country in which millions of people can expect to spend an increasing share of their lives in poor health is not just a recipe for a social crisis but a political one too. The latest figures are extraordinary. Healthy life expectancy in the United Kingdom has fallen to its lowest level since the present Office for National Statistics series began in 2011 to 2013. A boy born today can expect around 60.7 years of good health; for a girl, the figure is 60.9. Yet even these averages conceal the more disturbing story. In the most deprived areas of England, healthy life expectancy is just 49.8 years for men and 48.2 for women. In the least deprived areas, it reaches 69.2 and 68.5 years, respectively. Measured across the deprivation gradient, the gap is 19.3 years for men and 20.1 for women. Increasingly, Britain has become two countries separated by twenty years of healthy life. We usually describe this as a health inequality. That is correct but inadequate as an explanation. These figures are also a measure of political inequality: a biological record of where security has been withdrawn, public infrastructure allowed to decay, and entire communities exposed to conditions from which wealthier populations are largely protected. Earlier this year, I argued in Jacobin that the dominant political account of ill health performs a convenient act of misdirection. When obesity increases, governments talk about individual discipline. When diabetes becomes more prevalent, they talk about diet. When anxiety, addiction, or depression spread through poorer communities, they discover resilience. Structural conditions are translated into personal shortcomings; the political becomes behavioral. There is another danger in treating illness this way: if we understand population health only as the accumulated consequence of individual choices, we fail to recognize what sickness can tell us about the condition of society itself. Increasingly, it may also serve as a proxy measure of our politics, too. The Geography of Sickness Britain’s geography of poor health is stark. Places subjected to deindustrialization, poverty, and economic insecurity have carried a disproportionate burden of illness for decades. Indeed, research on Britain’s former coalfields, for example, has repeatedly identified persistent health deficits in communities left behind by manufactured industrial collapse. Recent research examining deaths from suicide, drugs, and alcohol in former mining communities in England and Wales found elevated mortality even after contemporary deprivation was taken into account. This matters because economic abandonment does not simply remove a wage packet. When an industry disappears, it can take with it the institutions anchored around it: trade unions, social clubs, apprenticeships, commercial centers, community organizations, and, eventually, younger generations themselves. Local tax bases weaken; public services contract; high streets empty; employment becomes more precarious. What begins as an economic shock becomes a social environment. The social environment, of course, in turn becomes a lived reality. For years, political scientists have attempted to explain the growth of the populist and radical right through two competing stories. One emphasizes material insecurity: deindustrialization, unemployment, austerity, and declining economic status. The other emphasizes cultural backlash: immigration, identity, and changing social values. The division has always been somewhat artificial. Economic insecurity changes how people experience social change; cultural resentment provides a language through which economic insecurity can be interpreted. Yet there is another neglected explanation: health. In 2021, Nolan Kavanagh, Anil Menon, and Justin Heinze analyzed every wave of the European Social Survey between 2002 and 2020. Their findings were striking. Respondents reporting worse health were significantly more likely to vote for right-wing populist parties. The association persisted after accounting for measures of economic vulnerability, cultural attitudes, life satisfaction, and satisfaction with the health system. Britain now has its own version of this finding. Anthony Laverty and Nicholas Hopkinson examined all 543 English constituencies following the 2024 general election. Constituencies electing Reform UK members of Parliament recorded the highest average prevalence of fifteen of the twenty health conditions studied. More important, across England, Reform vote share remained associated with several markers of poor health after adjustment for age, sex, and deprivation. A 10 percentage point increase in Reform vote share was associated with a 0.261 percentage point higher prevalence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a 0.113 percentage point increase in asthma, and a 1.479 percentage point increase in obesity. Yet we must resist the temptation to be reductionist in these findings. It is not simply that as people become sick, they move to the radical right. That conclusion would be both scientifically weak and politically confused. The English study is ecological. It tells us about constituencies, not the motivations of individual voters. The European research demonstrates an individual-level association, but association is not destiny. Neither proves that illness somehow creates authoritarian attitudes. But there is a question, if we scratch beneath the surface, that proves more useful and operationalizable: What if the forces producing poor health are also producing political revolt? One Crisis, Two Symptoms Researchers examining England and Wales found that areas experiencing larger rises in suicide and drug-related deaths before the Brexit referendum were also more likely to vote Leave. Yet once education and other socioeconomic characteristics were introduced, much of that statistical relationship disappeared. The authors’ conclusion was particularly important: worsening mortality and Brexit voting appeared to have similar antecedents. In summarized terms, sickness was not necessarily causing political rebellion. Both could be expressions of the same wound. Austerity provides perhaps the clearest example. The economist Thiemo Fetzer’s influential analysis of Britain’s post-2010 welfare reforms found that areas and individuals more exposed to austerity subsequently showed greater support for the UK Independence Party, stronger political dissatisfaction, and greater support for leaving the European Union. His counterfactual modeling went further, suggesting that without austerity the referendum could have produced a Remain majority. The finding is no longer peculiarly British. Research across Western democracies has shown that austerity disproportionately increases populist voting in economically vulnerable regions, with radical right parties benefiting particularly strongly in those areas. A major 2026 review of the political science literature reached a similar conclusion: austerity magnifies rather than protects people from social risk and, in doing so, increases support for nonmainstream and frequently populist parties among economically vulnerable voters. An economy is restructured. Security disappears. Welfare protection is withdrawn. Public institutions retreat. Health deteriorates. Political trust declines. Then, at the end of this process, commentators arrive to marvel at the irrational anger of the people who remain. When the State Becomes Something That Happens to You Poor health may deepen this estrangement in another way: it increases people’s exposure to institutions whose deterioration they experience directly. For somebody who is healthy and economically secure, government can remain relatively abstract. For somebody awaiting an operation, dependent upon disability support, caring for an ill parent, unable to obtain a general practitioner (GP) appointment, or negotiating an increasingly punitive welfare system, the state is not an abstraction. It is encountered repeatedly. The state should not be in a precarious triangulation of help, humiliation, or hampering. Research across nineteen Western European countries has found that people reporting poor health exhibit lower levels of political trust than those in good health. The relationship between health and political participation is more complicated, but no less important. European research suggests poorer health generally suppresses electoral turnout, while certain health problems can simultaneously encourage other forms of political activity. Illness, therefore, does not produce political passivity in any simple sense. It can exclude people from conventional democratic participation while intensifying grievance elsewhere. We mustn’t lose fact of this distinction: a person who no longer believes that established institutions represent them has not ceased to be political. They may simply become available to a different politics. The radical right understands this exceptionally well. Its political skill has been to recognize material experiences that liberal politics too often denies — and then supply a false explanation for them. The abandoned high street is real. The inaccessible GP is real. The insecure job is real. The sense that Westminster regards entire communities as little more than electoral scenery is often entirely rational. The migrant is made responsible for the hospital corridor; the asylum seeker for the housing shortage; the welfare claimant for fiscal scarcity. A political economy organized around inequality disappears from view, replaced by a morality play in which equally insecure groups are invited to fight over the remains. Now, this is not to downplay the grievance, which is very real; the target, however, is manufactured. Health Is Part of Democratic Infrastructure This should change how the Left thinks about public health. Health inequality is generally approached as a question of social justice: poorer people should not live shorter and sicker lives simply because they are poor. On its own terms, the argument holds, but there is another political reason to care. Good health is a part of the democratic infrastructure. Secure employment is democratic infrastructure. Social housing is democratic infrastructure. An adequately funded welfare state is democratic infrastructure. So are buses, libraries, youth centers, functioning local governments, and a health service that appears when people need it. These institutions do something more than redistribute resources. They provide daily evidence that collective action can improve ordinary life. The UK’s experiment in austerity provides a teachable moment: destroy enough collective action, and you dismantle the fabric of democracy. Recent European research provides support for the inverse proposition. Across sixteen Western European countries, populist parties performed worse where governments provided stronger income support to people experiencing unemployment; reductions in labor-market protection were associated with greater populist support, particularly among people directly exposed to economic insecurity. Yet this is not a lesson in welfare spending equaling political obedience; quite the opposite — it’s about the empowerment of individuals and enfranchisement of communities. And this empowerment and enfranchisement is, through the aforementioned determents of health, equitably distributed to the most deprived and vulnerable communities. There is no blood test for authoritarianism, and hardship carries no predetermined politics: it has produced trade unionism, socialism, mutual aid, and solidarity as readily as reaction. But suffering does demand an explanation. I have seen this repeatedly as a National Health Service doctor, when a consultation ostensibly about breathlessness, aches, and pains, or poorly controlled diabetes, quickly becomes a conversation about a cold home, insecure work, benefits, or housing; medicine can treat part of the problem, but not the conditions producing it. Yet patients also notice when the system works; when they are listened to, properly treated, and followed up with; and when a public institution does what it was built to do. That is why health inequality is also a democratic question: when institutions repeatedly fail, somebody will eventually explain why, and the danger lies in who supplies that explanation and whom they persuade people to blame. Population health is not merely an outcome of politics; it is one of its vital signs.

articles.content: HAPPY LABOR DAY: A FESTIVAL OF RESISTANCE WITH VERMONT MAY DAY STRONG This Labor Day, join Vermont May Day Strong and your friends, neighbors, and fellow workers for a Festival of Resistance. We'll have free food, music, activities, tabling, and a few brief speeches from Vermont workers standing up against the Trump regime and the billionaire class. Whether it's healthcare workers fighting for safe staffing at UVM Medical Center, Healthy Living workers resisting anti-democratic union busting, or migrant workers organizing for their right to dignified work free from attacks by ICE and Border Patrol, Vermont's workers are standing up, pushing back, and doing so together. The Festival of Resistance is an opportunity for us to celebrate the organizing we have done, the power we continue to build, and our past and future victories. All are welcome at this family-friendly event TODAY — Monday September 7 at 3:00pm at Battery Park in Burlington Learn more TAX THE RICH: MONTPELIER AND WINOOSKI CANVASSES IN SEPTEMBER: LOOKING AHEAD TO TOWN MEETING DAY 2027 BALLOT QUESTIONS Working Vermonters are being squeezed while the richest continue to benefit from tax cuts paid for by cuts to healthcare. Medicaid and ACA subsidies are on the chopping block, putting tens of thousands at risk. This is a choice. We can let working people carry the burden, or we can demand that the wealthiest pay their fair share. We are calling on the Vermont Legislature to pass legislation that raises taxes on the richest 5 percent, taxes wealth proceeds, and invests that revenue into affordable and accessible healthcare for all. Half measures are not enough. Policies that only target the top 1 percent or shift taxes around without raising new revenue will not meet this moment. We marched with workers on the picket line, joined our neighbors in advocating for the release of Pastor Steven Tendo, and kept doing what socialists do every month: organizing our workplaces and communities, building solidarity, and fighting for a Vermont that works for working people. articles.title: Germany’s Far Right Is Close to Power. Appeals to “Defend Democracy” Won’t Stop It.
articles.author: Thomas Zimmermann
articles.content: In Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt, local Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund ran on the slogan “Anything Is Possible.” Those same words could serve as the headline for political forecasts the day after the vote. For while the election produced a clear winner, it didn’t yield a definitive outcome. While the far-right AfD scored an impressive 43.8 percent of votes cast, it has not secured an absolute majority. Nor does the anti-AfD camp have a majority, as Sahra Wagenknecht’s party — Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BW), a split from the socialist Die Linke — stands in between the two sides. If the AfD’s Siegmund is to be elected Saxony-Anhalt’s minister-president, he still needs three extra lawmakers in the state parliament on his side. One possibility is that a few Christian Democrats (CDU) who sympathize with the AfD and want nothing to do with Die Linke might switch sides. With its 17.2 percent share, the CDU’s ability to bring people together seems to have hit a low point. Alternatively, the BSW, on 5.3 percent, could be key. Whether BSW will support the AfD, as feared by the anti-AfD camp, or simply cost Siegmund his outright majority (as the AfD itself warned before the election) remains to be seen. Die Linke did a lot worse than polls suggested, on 8.6 percent; the Social Democrats (SPD) did slightly better with 9.3 percent; and the Greens did significantly better with 8.9 percent. If the Greens had failed to win any seats, as seemed possible, the AfD would likely have secured an absolute majority. Groups advocating tactical voting will likely interpret this outcome as validation of their efforts. Yet this overlooks the main consequence of this politics of interchangeability within the “democratic camp.” For it is made up of four weak parties that, taken together, are barely as strong as the AfD alone. The fact that this kind of “defense of democracy” is close to bankruptcy is evident from what “democracy” is being defended against here. For this election saw a near-absolute majority, a record voter turnout of 76 percent, and an enormous mobilization of previous nonvoters, the vast majority of whom went to the AfD. Yes, Majorities Are Democratic The plight of the “defenders of democracy” was well-illustrated just before the election by the SPD’s top candidate, Armin Willingmann. During a preelection debate program, he attempted to portray the mere fact of a party pursuing an absolute majority as an inherently antidemocratic threat. You wonder how they come up with this stuff. Willingmann explained, “Since the founding of the Federal Republic [in 1949], we’ve had good experiences with not having single-party governments, or virtually no single-party governments. Compromise, seeking consensus, and balancing interests is the essence of our democracy.” Referring to Siegmund’s statement that he wanted to become minister-president only on the basis of an absolute majority, Willingmann warned: “I see this attempt to govern without compromise as a path toward authoritarianism.” Someone should remind him that in Saarland, his party comrade Anke Rehlinger is currently leading a single-party SPD government. But if compromise were, in itself, really so democratic, then politicians wouldn’t hate preelection questions about possible coalition options so much. After all, they certainly don’t dodge these questions out of “respect for the voters,” as they always claim. They do so because they know they are elected for their broader ambitions and not out of eagerness to make compromises with opposing parties — compromises that inevitably end up in the trash can. In fact, the opposite is true: parties that would rather form a coalition than govern alone are rightly suspected of not actually intending to implement their platforms, and of not really being too keen to change the unpopular status quo. No Democracy Without Visions The problem is not that the AfD is striving for an absolute majority. Rather, the failure lies with the other parties, which seemingly have no convincing visions to offer. The SPD has no social democracy, Die Linke no democratic socialism, the BSW no “social justice and sound economics,” the Free Democrats no special economic zones, the CDU no status quo, and the Greens no war with Russia capable of inspiring the masses. Now the bill has come due: of all parties, the antidemocratic AfD is the one managing to inspire the disillusioned masses to participate in democracy. On election night, probably no one used the word “democracy” as much as the AfD’s Siegmund. Any serious left-wing strategy is based on the conviction that the broad majority, which has lost faith in politics, can be mobilized through the struggle for a different society. The AfD has now proven that it is possible to mobilize nonvoters. It remains the Left’s job to do better in this regard than the Right. This society needs a different vision for the future, one that goes beyond both the ailing status quo and the AfD’s offer of a return to an imagined past. Anyone who wants to fight for democracy should not rely on the constant compromise of many small and shrinking parties but should instead try to inspire the people to embrace their own vision. For in the long run, there can be no “defense of democracy” against absolute majorities and massive mobilization of nonvoters.

articles.title: Rust Belt Rising
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Hannah W. The first ever Rust Belt Rising conference was held on August 15th and 16th here in Rochester. This was organized by Workers Assembly of Rochester (WAR), an independent organization of local labor activists, including DSA members, union staffers and organizers. Local labor leaders, rank and file members and members of community organizations gathered to discuss and learn about the role of the labor movement in Rochester, and how we can move it to be more militant and left. Opening Keynote The opening keynote was a panel containing Colin, an organizer with the Teamsters Local 118, Christina, President of the Federation of Social Workers and Max from Buffalo DSA and Field Director for the Adam Bojak Campaign. The topic was How to Build an Independent Worker Program, which I think is a relevant topic given the current political state. Comrade Max talked about the role labor plays in elections, citing the work he and other comrades have done for Adam Bojak for the 149th assembly. While many unions did endorse Bojak, “We want labor to be a partner, not just a stamp”. Max posed to the audience what difference does union endorsement make, especially if they’re not turning out members for electoral races. While they may provide money for mailers, having people to knock doors is the most effective way to reach voters. He also spoke about the need to move away from the Democratic Party and not waste time and resources trying to take over local Democratic committees. Starting to run your own candidates, and that a sense of “ownership” will be felt by the members. We’ve seen this with Clarie Valdez as an example of a rank and file union member and DSA member who ran for state assembly and now Congress. Colin spoke about the union endorsement process that candidates go through and asked if that process is democratic. Do members have the ability to ask questions of the candidates? Do members have the final vote for the endorsement? Colin noted that this gatekeeping of democracy comes from entrenched union leadership wanting to keep power, rather than allow the rank and file to make decisions. We’ve seen this play out with unions endorsing candidates like Joe Morelle. Colin also spoke on how unions think we’re organizing to support candidates but oftentimes, the politicians are the ones “organizing us.” Christina spoke about beating apathy by having continuous conversations with membership. From engaging them in endorsements to participating in co-governance with endorsed candidates. This looks like holding town halls with electeds, starting mobilization committees, and shifting the union perspective to an organizing mindset. While not all members have the same perspective, this will lead to a more engaged membership. She also talked about the need to work with community groups to build strength and solidarity. Overall I was impressed with the panelists’ perspectives on building out an independent program. This is a long term goal to achieve, but I think the first step is educating the rank and file. In doing so, we can hopefully have members active in electoral campaigns, and end the cycle of endorsing candidates who don’t stand with the working class. Workshops Throughout the conference there were 5 different blocks of workshops with 16 unique workshops. Overall the variety in the programming was impressive, from union contracts, to organizing history and current politics. Get a Job to Organize: Salting This was about salting a workplace. For those unfamiliar with the term, Salting is getting a job with the explicit purpose of unionizing the workplace. Doing so is not an easy task as you have to build out a list of who would want to join in this effort. The workshop went over what it takes to salt, the qualities of a good salt and what the process may look like. The main skill being communication, as salters will have numerous conversations with their co-workers. Colin mentioned a learning on his end of making sure the timeline is communicated to the salter before taking a job. An example is Amazon as this is a long term operation that is 15 – 20 years and a salter should be willing to commit for several years. In addition, he spoke to the desire to have salts stay through the unionization effort and become shop stewards. In doing so, it can ensure the union stays militant and left-leaning. DSA has its own Workers Organizing Workers program, which will train members on how to salt. If you are a member of DSA and interested in salting, please reach out to the chapter and we can get you connected. Secrets of a Successful Organizer: Beating Apathy Kari from Labor Notes gave this training on how to beat apathy. When we think about organizing, we need to think about our list of members as a bullseye (pictured below). This helps determine the level of membership involvement in a given union/organization. The training covered different reasons members wouldn’t get engaged and proposed solutions to counter that. Once we’ve built out our list, the training went over common barriers as to why people might not engage. These four barriers were fear, hopelessness, division and confusion. The room was ask to split amongst those four barriers. In each group, we were asked to give an example of our word and then provide solutions to beating this. Secrets of a Successful Organizer: Assembling your Dream Team Assembling your Dream Team is a continuation from the previous session of Beating Apathy. This workshop went over how to identify leaders within a workplace and bring them into your organizing committee. From there building out a list of your workplace and identifying your members/coworkers who are core, active, disengaged, supportive and hostile. Kari stressed the importance of listwork to identify members that could be leaders. The workshop had us go through two scenarios. One where we were trying to organize a workplace to wear stickers. This was to get us to think of mapping out our workplace, who works there, who talks to who. From there we went over ways to identify leaders in the workplace. Lastly we went through a scenario of identifying leaders for an organizing committee at a hotel. My work with member engagement has familiarized me with the bullseye method. While it is tedious to go through around 550 records, it is important work. Identifying where members lie helps us determine who we need to reengage with and potentially turn into active members. In doing so, we can build leadership and bring members up within the chapter. What NOT to do if you want an active membership The final workshop I attended was things not to do if you want membership engaged. Colin led this workshop and was mainly posing questions to the audience. The first was about involvement and why members don’t engage or get involved. Answers ranged from cliques and gatekeeping to lack of understanding from membership. Second was phrases used that people have heard. Responses included “That’s how it’s done,” “That’s not how it works.” Of the responses, it was noted that sometimes these are valid. On the other hand, we also must think about what message that conveys to membership. Does it allow them to engage or eventually solve the issue on their own? The session ended with asks for all the organizers present to: Invite Listen Delegate Train Support Move on The workshop for me helped change my perspective about how I answer questions members may direct at me. Instead of taking on the work myself, am I able to delegate and empower said members. In doing so this can help create a more involved membership and also build the skills members need to become leaders. Day 1 Closing: New Union Organizing The Day 1 closing was a panel about new union organizing. This included RUNAP, Webster & Penfield EMT (Teamsters 118?), U of R Grad Labor Union (SEIU 200) and Home Healthcare Workers (1199 SEIU). Each of the panelists were given the same set of questions to answer. One question that stood out to me was about tactics they tried that fell flat. For the Webster & Penfield EMT, it was them not anticipating how aggressive the union busting campaign would be. While they did prepare, it was far more hostile than what they expected. The same was also said for the U of R grad union, as UofR changed tactics once Trump was re-elected in 2024. Matt from RUNAP mentioned ensuring that people stay involved and enthusiastic, but their expectations don’t go beyond what the union can actually do. This leads to needing to educate membership. Lastly, Mike from 1199 SEIU emphasized the importance of tools and speed for organizing the ~200,000 home healthcare workers in New York who are now eligible for union membership. Through organizing, workers can create power and pressure on the boss and win. While some, like the Grad Union are still waiting to be recognized, they were able to win wage increases through organizing. With the continued organizing of unions in the Rochester area, we can build worker power and fight for what is rightfully ours. Day 2 Closing: Upcoming Labor Fights The final panel of the conference was on upcoming labor fights here in the Rochester area. This included 1199 SEIU, SEIU 200 and RUNAP. This covered the two largest employers in the area: University of Rochester and Rochester Regional Health. As stated during the panel, these employers set the economic health of the Rochester region. If they underpay their workers, it brings down wages across the entire community. Part of the panel discussed bargaining units and what the main concerns of their members are. Overall, the top concern was health care and benefits. It’s no secret that companies have moved the American population over to high deductible plans to allow wealth transfer to insurance CEOs. I asked the panelists how the NY Health Act (Single payer health care) would benefit them during bargaining. The panelists were all in favor of the bill noting it would allow them to not spend the fight on health care, and bargain for other benefits such as child care. Overall Thoughts First I want to recognize the organizing effort that went into this by my fellow WAR members. From reaching out to unions, to getting panels and booking the venue. I appreciate the work that was done to make this a successful event. I think for the first ever conference I enjoyed going to it and did learn from it and view it as a success. From what I talked with others, some of the workshops could be improved. However I think that is somewhat standard for conferences given that not every workshop will be a success. Perhaps more vetting and walkthroughs of the workshops might be helpful prior to the conference. In addition, evaluations of the workshops can also help the presenters as well. Outside of ROC DSA there were a handful of other DSA members that attended the event. The beginning panel had two DSA members on it calling out socialism explicitly. I think as DSA we should continue to build relationships with members of unions. I think conferences like this are a great opportunity to learn more about local organizing efforts and have direct conversations with union members. To me, the best part was the opening panel as it spoke to the need to divert resources and power from the establishment. In doing so, we can elect people who will actually support and fight for the working class, rather than use us for a photo op. This conference helped reshape the way I view myself as an organizer and the actions I take. The people I talked to were in some form of elected leadership or staffers, with some unelected rank and file members. My hope with this conference is to have more unelected rank and file members join in the coming years. I was impressed with how the conference went and I’m looking forward to the next one. The post Rust Belt Rising first appeared on Rochester Red Star .
